passages.t: ‘The nations have invaded Your inheritance’: no one to bury the dead
passages.happening:
The heading reads, “A Psalm of Asaph” (verse 1). The psalm opens in ruins. “The nations, O God, have invaded Your inheritance; they have defiled Your holy temple and reduced Jerusalem to rubble” (verse 1). The dead lie in the open, food for birds and wild animals (verse 2). There is, they say, “no one to bury the dead” (verse 3). The neighbours laugh (verse 4).

Then come the questions. “How long, O LORD? Will You be angry forever?” (verse 5). The people ask God to pour out his anger on the nations that have destroyed them (verses 6 to 7). They also ask for mercy for themselves. “Do not hold past sins against us; let Your compassion come quickly, for we are brought low” (verse 8). They pray, “deliver us and atone for our sins, for the sake of Your name” (verse 9).

They pray for prisoners and those sentenced to die (verse 11). They ask God to pay back their neighbours ‘sevenfold’ (verse 12). The psalm ends with a promise: “Then we Your people, the sheep of Your pasture, will thank You forever” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 79 is a twin of Psalm 74. Both grieve the temple's destruction, which most scholars place in 587 or 586 BC, as the note on Psalm 74 explains. Psalm 74 looked at the burned building. Psalm 79 looks at the people: the bodies in the streets with no one left to bury them.

In the ancient world, to leave the dead unburied was one of the worst shames that could happen. The law of Moses named it among the curses that would follow if Israel turned from God (Deuteronomy 28:26). So the people feel both the grief and the shame.

Notice that this prayer does not only blame the enemy. It also confesses: ‘Do not hold past sins against us’, ‘atone for our sins’. The people know that their own unfaithfulness is part of the story. They ask for mercy for themselves, and justice on those who killed their families.

Verses 6 and 7 are almost the same words as Jeremiah 10:25. Either one drew on the other, or both drew on a prayer the people already knew.
passages.later:
Jeremiah prays, “Pour out Your wrath on the nations that do not acknowledge You” (Jeremiah 10:25), in nearly the words of verse 6.

In Revelation the martyrs cry out in heaven, “How long, O Lord, holy and true, until You avenge our blood” (Revelation 6:10). And Paul tells the church, “Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for God's wrath” (Romans 12:19).
passages.hard: Is it right to pray for God's anger on other nations, and for sevenfold payback (verses 6 and 12)? The book page's part on the cursing psalms sets out how Christians read prayers like these, and these notes do not choose between those readings. Two things are plain. The prayer hands vengeance to God rather than taking it. And ‘the nations’ here are the armies that burned Jerusalem in that ancient war. The psalm gives no one the right to name any people today as its enemy.
passages.asks:
If you have seen what was precious to you torn down, this psalm lets you bring God both your grief and your anger. It also teaches you to bring your own sins in the same breath. That is a hard and honest way to pray.

Pray for the ‘captives’ and those ‘condemned to death’ (verse 11) in our own world: those in prison, those in war, those with no one to speak for them.
